title: Long-Term Care and Medicare: What Is and Is Not Covered
bigPicture: Medicare does not pay for long-term care, so you pay the cost unless you have another source such as Medicaid or private long-term care insurance.
whatYouNeedToKnow: Long-term care, also called custodial care, covers medical and non-medical help for people with a chronic illness or disability. Most of it is help with activities of daily living, such as personal care, home-delivered meals, adult day health care, and transportation.
Medicare does not pay for long-term care, whether it is in a nursing home or in the community. Medicare Supplement Insurance (Medigap) does not cover it either.
Long-term care is different from skilled nursing facility care, which Medicare does cover under its own rules.
You may qualify for Medicaid help if you meet your state's eligibility rules.
You can also choose to buy private long-term care insurance.
Long-term care can be received at home, in the community, in assisted living, or in a nursing home.

If you itemize on your taxes, premiums for qualified long-term care insurance are listed by the IRS among deductible medical expenses, but only the part of your total medical costs above 7.5% of your adjusted gross income is deductible.
commonMistakesToAvoid: Assuming Medicare or Medigap pays for long-term care. They do not.
Mixing up long-term care (custodial care) with skilled nursing facility care, which Medicare covers separately.
Waiting to learn about your options until you or a family member needs care.
actionSteps: Read the Medicare.gov long-term care page listed below.
Look up your state's Medicaid rules for long-term care help.
If you think about private long-term care insurance, ask for the policy terms in writing and compare more than one offer.
Talk with your family about what kind of care you would want.
